whats the difference between a primary and secondary source? have a history paper and my teacher keeps marking me on it

A primary source is firsthand evidence from the time period you're studying, like letters, diaries, speeches, photos, or government records. A secondary source is someone's later analysis or interpretation of that evidence, like textbooks, journal articles, or documentaries. Example: a soldier's letter is primary; a historian's book about the war using that letter is secondary. In your paper, use primary sources as your evidence and secondary ones to support or contrast your argument.

messages.content:
Personal statement v3 - feedback from Mr. Okafor (2026-11-09)
Word count: 712 (limit 650)
Hartwell University EA deadline: Nov 20
Legend: MUST = fix before submitting, SHOULD = strongly suggested, NICE = optional

== Paragraph 1 (opening) ==
1. [NICE] Love the soldering iron burning your thumb in the first line.
2. [SHOULD] 'Ever since I was young' is a cliche. Cut that sentence.
3. [NICE] Strong hook. Keep the radio-repair detail.

== Paragraph 2 ==
4. [MUST] This paragraph is a list of clubs. Common App already has an activities section. Replace with one concrete story.
5. [SHOULD] Say what actually broke on the robotics drive train and how you fixed it.
6. [SHOULD] Too many passive constructions ('it was decided', 'the arm was built').
7. [NICE] 'Synergy' - delete.

== Paragraph 3 ==
8. [MUST] This is your best paragraph (grandfather's workshop) but it is buried. Move it up to paragraph 2.
9. [SHOULD] Show, don't tell: 'I learned patience' -> describe the moment.
10. [SHOULD] Keep only one line of dialogue with your grandfather.
11. [NICE] Tense shifts in sentence 4.

== Paragraph 4 ==
12. [MUST] Cut roughly 60 words here to reach the limit.
13. [SHOULD] The hackathon sentence runs 58 words. Split it.
14. [NICE] Typo: 'recieved'.
15. [SHOULD] Explain what the app does in one sentence for a non-technical reader.

== Paragraph 5 (ending) ==
16. [MUST] 'And that is why I want to change the world' is a cliche. End on the workshop image instead.
17. [SHOULD] Don't restate your thesis.
18. [NICE] Consider a shorter final sentence.

== General ==
19. [MUST] Total is 712 words; need 650 or fewer. Cut at least 62.
20. [SHOULD] Vary sentence length.
21. [NICE] Read it aloud before sending v4.
22. [SHOULD] Don't name-drop Hartwell in the body; save it for the supplement.

== Logistics ==
 Send v4 by Mon Nov 16 (email is fine)
 Next meeting: Tue Nov 17, 3:15pm, Room 214
 Bring a printed copy for the read-aloud pass.

There are 22 comments, but only 5 are MUST fixes: (1) replace the club-list paragraph 2 with one concrete story, (2) move the grandfather's workshop paragraph up to paragraph 2, (3) cut ~60 words from paragraph 4, (4) rewrite the 'change the world' ending to close on the workshop image, and (5) get from 712 to 650 words total. Fixing 1, 3 and 4 will mostly solve the word count. He wants v4 by Monday Nov 16, and you meet Tuesday at 3:15pm in Room 214 with a printed copy.

quick q, if i have 3 hours of study time and 4 subjects, is it better to do 45 min each or do like 2 subjects deep? i have chem and calc tests thursday, english and apush quizzes friday

Split it by what's due first and how hard it is. Since chem and calc tests are Thursday, give them the deep time: about 75 minutes each, with a 5-10 minute break in between. Then do English and APUSH in short passes of 15-20 minutes each, or save them for Thursday night after the tests, since quizzes usually need less prep. Switching subjects between blocks also helps retention.
ok but what if im tired by the second block

Put the harder subject first, while you're fresh. Do the calc problems first, since practice problems take the most focus, and chem second, where review is more about recall. Use a short walk or snack before the second block. If you're still dragging, switch to active recall like flashcards or self-quizzing instead of rereading.

whats the difference between a stack and a queue? apcsa test tmrw and i keep mixing them up

A stack is last-in, first-out (LIFO): you add and remove at the same end, like a pile of plates. Operations are push, pop, and peek.

A queue is first-in, first-out (FIFO): you add at the back and remove from the front, like a line at a store. Operations are enqueue (add), dequeue (remove), and peek.

Tip: stack = newest comes out first, queue = oldest comes out first.

quick q for my lit review: whats the difference between a systematic review and a meta-analysis? i keep mixing them up

A systematic review is a structured, reproducible way of finding and evaluating all the studies on a question. You define search terms, inclusion criteria and quality checks up front, and then summarize the findings, often in words and tables.

A meta-analysis is a statistical technique that pools numerical results from several studies into one overall effect size. It often sits inside a systematic review, but it isn't required. If the studies are too different to combine, you can still do a systematic review without one.

So every meta-analysis should be based on a systematic review, but not every systematic review includes a meta-analysis.

whats the difference between a primary and secondary source? my history teacher keeps marking me down on it

A primary source is firsthand evidence from the time you're studying, like letters, diaries, speeches, photos, or census records. A secondary source analyzes or interprets those events later, like textbooks, documentaries, or journal articles written by historians.

A quick test: did the author experience or create it during the event, or are they describing it afterward? Context matters, too. A 1990s history book is secondary for the Civil War but primary for how people in the 1990s viewed it.

messages.name: read_file
messages.content:
PERSONAL STATEMENT - PEER REVIEW NOTES (draft 3, 712 words)
Reviewer: Ms. Dalton | Date: 2026-11-10

OVERALL
1. Strong voice. The bakery-at-5am opening is the best thing in the essay.
2. Word limit is 650. You are at 712. Need to cut about 65 words.
3. Theme (learning to slow down) is clear by paragraph 2.
4. The ending feels rushed compared to the opening.

PARAGRAPH 1
5. Great sensory detail: flour on the scale, the oven timer.
6. 'I have always been a person who' - cut this phrase.
7. Sentence 4 is 46 words. Split it.
8. 'recieve' -> 'receive'.

PARAGRAPH 2
9. Good turn when the first loaf collapses. Keep.
10. Comma splice in sentence 3.
11. 'passion' appears here. See note 24.
12. Dialogue with Grandpa Leo is lovely but runs long. Trim two lines.

PARAGRAPH 3
13. This is the longest paragraph (218 words). Consider splitting.
14. Tense shifts from past to present midway ('I stand at the counter').
15. The debate club section does not connect to the theme.
16. If you keep debate, tie it to patience in arguments.
17. Otherwise cut it entirely; that saves about 70 words.
18. 'definately' -> 'definitely'.

PARAGRAPH 4
19. Nice moment: teaching your cousin to knead dough.
20. Show more of what you learned, less telling.
21. 'Slow and steady wins the race' is a cliche. Cut.
22. The Thoreau quote feels borrowed. Your own line is stronger.

CONCLUSION
23. Circle back to the 5am bakery. Echo the opening image.
24. 'Passion' is used 4 times total. Vary it or cut two.
25. Final sentence is vague ('I am excited for the future').
26. Replace with something specific about what you will bring to college.

STYLE
27. Several sentences begin with 'I'. Vary openings.
28. Watch adverbs: 'really', 'very', 'truly'.
29. Read aloud once to catch rhythm problems.

MINOR
30. Hyphenate 'five-o'clock' only when used as adjective.
31. Check capitalization of 'Grandpa' when used as a name.
32. Spell out numbers under ten.

PRIORITY ORDER (my suggestion)
A. Cut to 650 words (debate paragraph is the easiest cut).
B. Fix tense shift in paragraph 3.
C. Rewrite the conclusion to echo the opening.
D. Proofread typos and clichés.

RESUBMIT BY: 2026-11-20
Nice work overall. This is close.

Ms. Dalton likes it overall, especially the 5am bakery opening, and says it's close. What to fix, in her priority order:
1. Cut from 712 to 650 words. The debate club section (about 70 words, doesn't fit the theme) is the easiest cut.
2. Fix the past-to-present tense shift in paragraph 3 and split that 218-word paragraph.
3. Rewrite the conclusion to echo the bakery opening, replacing the vague "excited for the future" line.
4. Proofread: "recieve", "definately", the comma splice in paragraph 2, and cut the clichés ("slow and steady wins the race", the Thoreau quote). "Passion" appears 4 times, so cut two.

She wants the resubmission by 2026-11-20.

messages.name: read_file
messages.content:
SEARCH: school start time adolescent sleep (saved 2027-01-18)

[1] Delayed School Start Times and Adolescent Sleep: A Systematic Review
    Authors: Hana Lindqvist, R. Abara | Sleep Policy Journal 2023 | Cited by 214
    Type: systematic review (18 studies)
    Note: Most studies show +25 to +77 min weeknight sleep after delay

[2] My kid hates mornings - parenting forum thread
    Source: forum.example.net | 2022
    Type: opinion

[3] Later Start, Better Grades? Evidence from 9 Districts
    Authors: Marcus Telford | Education Economics Review 2022 | Cited by 97
    Type: observational, district data
    Note: small GPA gains, strongest in low-income districts

[4] Circadian Phase Shift in Puberty: A Longitudinal Study
    Authors: S. Okafor, J. Brandt | Chronobiology Letters 2021 | Cited by 330
    Type: longitudinal, n=412
    Note: Explains biological basis for later sleep onset

[5] Top 10 Sleep Hacks for Teens
    Source: wellness.example.com | 2024
    Type: blog

[6] Start Time Change and Car Crash Rates in Teen Drivers
    Authors: D. Ferreira | Traffic Safety Quarterly 2020 | Cited by 156
    Type: observational, state crash data
    Note: crash rate for 16-18 yr olds dropped 16% after 1 hr delay

[7] Sleep Duration and Mood in High School Students
    Authors: L. Nakamura | Journal of Adolescent Wellbeing 2019 | Cited by 48
    Type: survey, n=230, single school
    Note: small sample, self-reported

[8] Delayed Start Times: A Cost Analysis of Bus Rescheduling
    Authors: P. Whitcombe | Public Finance Notes 2023 | Cited by 31
    Type: cost analysis, 5 districts
    Note: costs vary widely; some districts saved money

[9] Do Teens Really Need 9 Hours? (news article)
    Source: news.example.org | 2023
    Type: news

[10] Retraction notice: Start Time and Attendance in Rural Schools
     Source: Education Economics Review | 2021
     Note: original study retracted for data errors

END OF RESULTS (10 items)

Start with these: #1 (Lindqvist & Abara systematic review, 18 studies, +25 to +77 min of sleep, the strongest overview), #4 (Okafor & Brandt, the puberty circadian-shift study, best for the biology), and #6 (Ferreira, 16% drop in teen crashes, a strong real-world outcome). Also useful: #3 (Telford, grade effects) and #8 (Whitcombe, bus costs) if you cover the tradeoffs. Skip #2, #5 and #9 (forum, blog and news), and #7 is weak because it's a single school with n=230. Avoid #10 entirely, since that study was retracted for data errors.

whats the difference between a systematic review and a meta-analysis? writing a paper intro and i keep mixing them up

A systematic review is a structured, reproducible search and appraisal of all the studies on a question, using set inclusion criteria. It can be purely narrative.

A meta-analysis is a statistical step that pools the numerical results from multiple studies into one combined effect estimate. Many systematic reviews include a meta-analysis, but not all do, and a meta-analysis only makes sense when the studies are similar enough to combine.

whats the difference between a stack and a queue? we have a quiz in APCS tmrw

A stack is last-in, first-out (LIFO): you add and remove from the same end, like a pile of plates. Main operations are push, pop and peek.

A queue is first-in, first-out (FIFO): you add at the back (enqueue) and remove from the front (dequeue), like a line at a store.

Typical uses: stacks for undo, recursion/call stack and expression parsing; queues for breadth-first search, task scheduling and buffering. In Java, use Deque (e.g. ArrayDeque) for stacks and Queue (e.g. LinkedList) for queues.
ok and what's the big O for each op

With a sensible implementation (linked list or array-backed deque):

Stack: push, pop, peek are all O(1).
Queue: enqueue, dequeue, peek are all O(1).

Searching for an arbitrary element in either is O(n). One gotcha: a queue built on a plain array where dequeue shifts everything down makes dequeue O(n), so quizzes sometimes ask about that.

why does this keep growing?? 

def add(item, bucket=[]):
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket

add(1) gives [1] then add(2) gives [1, 2]

Python evaluates default arguments once, when the function is defined, not on each call. So every call that omits `bucket` shares the same list object.

The usual fix is a `None` default:

def add(item, bucket=None):
    if bucket is None:
        bucket = []
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket

Now each call without `bucket` gets a fresh list. The same trap applies to dicts, sets, and any other mutable default.
ah makes sense. also is there a quick git alias to undo the last commit but keep my changes

Yes, use a soft reset. Add this to ~/.zshrc if you want a shell alias:

alias uncommit='git reset --soft HEAD~1'

Or as a git alias:

git config --global alias.uncommit 'reset --soft HEAD~1'

This moves HEAD back one commit and leaves the changes staged. Use `--mixed` (the default) instead if you want them unstaged. Only do this on commits you haven't pushed. If you already pushed, use `git revert HEAD` instead.

== Reader 1: Ms. Adeyemi (English teacher) ==

== Reader 2: Jonah (friend) ==

P4: Lost me. Too many metaphors.

P5: Last line feels like a motivational poster.

P3: Keep the dialogue; trim the quote after.
P3: Typo: "recieved" -> "received".
P4: Metaphor pileup. Pick one and commit.
P4: "kneeded" -> "kneaded".
P5: Ending is generic. Return to the burnt loaf image instead.
P5: Last sentence "I am ready for anything" - cut.
General: Strongest when specific, weakest when abstract.

- Try ending on the burnt loaf
- Scholarship version due Dec 1
- Ask Ms. Adeyemi for one more read
- Fix typos last
- Maybe cut the 1962 sentence?
- Check if Nonno should be Grandpa for clarity
- Trim P3 quote to one line

- Keep: the burnt sourdough opening, the grandfather dialogue in P3, and your funny, specific voice.

whats the difference between git merge and git rebase, like when would i actually pick one

Merge combines two branches by creating a merge commit, keeping the full history exactly as it happened. Rebase replays your commits on top of another branch, giving a linear history but rewriting those commits (new hashes).

Rule of thumb: rebase your own local feature branch onto main to tidy it up before opening a PR; merge when integrating shared branches or anything others have already pulled. Never rebase commits you've pushed and others are using.

is it ok to cite a preprint on arXiv in my paper? or does it have to be peer reviewed

Yes, you can cite arXiv preprints, but label them clearly as preprints (include the arXiv ID) since they haven't been peer reviewed. Check your instructor's or venue's rules; some prefer peer-reviewed sources for key claims.

If a preprint has since been published in a journal, cite the published version instead. For important claims, say in the text that the finding is preliminary.

messages.content:
Retrieval Practice vs. Restudying: What the Evidence Shows
Learning Science Digest, Department of Cognitive Science, Example University
Author: Dr. Marguerite Oyelaran. Published 2025-09-12. Updated 2026-11-03.

OVERVIEW
This review summarizes 31 experiments (total N = 4,208) comparing retrieval practice (self-testing) with restudying (rereading) for long-term retention.

KEY FINDINGS
1. Across the 31 experiments, retrieval practice outperformed restudying on delayed tests in 26 (84%).
2. The average effect size on delayed tests was d = 0.52 (95% CI 0.41 to 0.63).
3. On immediate tests (within 10 minutes), restudying was equal or slightly better in 12 experiments.
4. The advantage grows with delay: at 1 week, mean d = 0.61; at 2 days, mean d = 0.44.
5. Feedback after retrieval attempts raised the average effect to d = 0.68.

SAMPLE CHARACTERISTICS
- Undergraduates: 19 experiments
- Middle and high school students: 8 experiments
- Adults over 50: 4 experiments
- Materials: word lists (9), prose passages (12), science concepts (7), math procedures (3)
- Most studies were run in the US (22) and Europe (7); only 2 elsewhere.

MODERATORS
- Format: short-answer retrieval beat multiple-choice by a small margin (d difference 0.09).
- Spacing: retrieval spaced over several days beat massed retrieval in 7 of 8 comparisons.
- Difficulty: effects were largest when retrieval was challenging but successful (about 60-80% correct).
- Complex material: effects were smaller for math procedures (mean d = 0.31).

LIMITATIONS
- Many classroom studies lacked random assignment (11 of 31).
- Publication bias cannot be ruled out; a funnel plot showed mild asymmetry.
- Most delayed tests were within 2 weeks. Evidence beyond 1 month is limited (5 experiments).
- Participants in lab studies were often paid volunteers, who may be more motivated than typical students.

PRACTICAL IMPLICATIONS
- Replace some rereading with self-quizzing.
- Use feedback after each attempt.
- Space sessions across days.
- Students often believe rereading works better; metacognitive judgments favored restudying in 21 of 24 studies that measured them.

PRIMARY SOURCES CITED (selected)
- Hallworth, R., & Teng, L. (2019). Testing versus rereading in prose learning. Journal of Applied Memory, 12(3), 201-219.
- Brandvold, S. (2021). Feedback timing and the testing effect. Learning and Instruction Review, 8(1), 44-60.
- Mwangi, P., et al. (2022). Retrieval practice in secondary classrooms. Educational Psych Quarterly, 33(2), 115-138.
- Oyelaran, M. (2024). Metacognitive illusions in study choice. Cognition Letters, 19(4), 301-317.

HOW TO CITE THIS REVIEW
Oyelaran, M. (2025). Retrieval practice vs. restudying: What the evidence shows. Learning Science Digest. https://lsd.example.edu/reviews/retrieval-vs-restudy

Note: This is a narrative review, not a peer-reviewed article. Readers should consult the primary sources.

The Learning Science Digest review (Oyelaran, 2025) fits well: it covers 31 experiments (N = 4,208), and retrieval practice beat restudying on delayed tests in 26 of them, with an average d = 0.52 (CI 0.41 to 0.63). The advantage grows with delay (d = 0.61 at 1 week), feedback raises it to 0.68, and restudying is equal or slightly better on immediate tests. Limitations include 11 non-randomized studies, mild publication bias, and little evidence beyond 1 month.

One caveat: the page says it's a narrative review, not peer-reviewed, so for a lit review you should cite the primary studies it lists (e.g. Hallworth & Teng, 2019; Mwangi et al., 2022) and use this page as a guide. Want me to pull the other two search results too?

PERSONAL STATEMENT REVIEW - Ms. Albright - v3 - 2027-04-12
Scholarship: Hartwell Foundation Community Scholar | limit 650 words | current 702

Strong voice. The radio-repair opening is the best thing in the draft.
The middle drags and reads like a resume in places.

== PARAGRAPH 1 (opening) ==
1. Keep the first sentence exactly as is.
2. "ever since I was little" - cut, adds nothing.
3. The soldering burn detail is great. Add one more sensory detail (smell?).
4. Move the sentence about your grandmother's station (WKLD) up before the burn.

== PARAGRAPH 2 ==
5. Good transition into the robotics team.
6. "I learned a lot about teamwork" is telling, not showing. Replace with the scene where the drive train failed at regionals.
7. Two uses of "passionate" in this paragraph.
8. Cut the list of competitions; keep only the regional one.

== PARAGRAPH 3 ==
9. This is the resume paragraph.

whats the difference between a primary and secondary source? my history teacher keeps marking me down for mixing them up in my bibliography

A primary source is firsthand evidence from the time or person you're studying: letters, diaries, speeches, photos, official records, raw data, interviews you conducted. A secondary source analyzes or interprets primary sources after the fact: textbooks, journal articles, documentaries, biographies.

Quick test: did the author witness or create the thing you're studying? If so, it's primary. If they're explaining or summarizing it, it's secondary. The same item can be either depending on your topic. A 1990s news article is secondary for a paper on the Civil War but primary for a paper on how the media covered the 1990s.

whats the difference between git merge and git rebase, i keep mixing them up on my side project

Both combine work from one branch into another, but they handle history differently.

- merge: creates a new merge commit that joins the two branches. History stays exactly as it happened, but can get branchy.
- rebase: replays your branch's commits on top of the target branch, rewriting them as new commits. History is linear and clean.

Rule of thumb: rebase your own local feature branch to catch up with main, merge when bringing it into main, and never rebase commits you've already pushed that others use.
so if i already pushed my feature branch but nobody else is on it, rebase is fine?

Yes, that's fine as long as you're the only one using the branch. After rebasing you'll need to push with `git push --force-with-lease`, which is safer than plain `--force` because it refuses to overwrite commits you haven't seen.

whats the difference between git merge and git rebase? i keep getting told to rebase my feature branch before opening a PR for my discord bot repo

Both combine work from two branches, but they do it differently.

- merge: creates a new merge commit that joins the two histories. Nothing is rewritten, but the log gets branchy.
- rebase: replays your branch's commits on top of the target branch (e.g. main), giving a straight, linear history. It rewrites your commits, so they get new hashes.

Before a PR, people ask you to rebase so your commits sit cleanly on top of the latest main:

git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main

If you've already pushed the branch, you'll need git push --force-with-lease afterward. Only rebase branches that you alone are working on, never shared ones like main.
ok and if i hit conflicts mid-rebase?

Git pauses at the conflicting commit. Fix the files, then:

git add <files>
git rebase --continue

Other options: git rebase --skip drops that commit, and git rebase --abort puts everything back to how it was before you started. Abort is a safe escape hatch if it gets messy.

what's the difference between BibTeX and BibLaTeX, quick lookup pls. i keep mixing them up for my thesis template

messages.name: web_search
messages.content: [{"title":"BibLaTeX vs BibTeX: which should you use?","url":"https://tex.example.org/biblatex-vs-bibtex","snippet":"BibTeX is the older bibliography processor with .bst style files. BibLaTeX is a LaTeX package that handles formatting itself, uses Biber as backend, and supports full Unicode and more entry types."},{"title":"Choosing a bibliography tool","url":"https://docs.example.net/latex/bibliography","snippet":"BibLaTeX styles are customized in LaTeX rather than in .bst files, making them much easier to modify."}]

BibTeX is the older processor that formats citations using .bst style files. BibLaTeX is a newer LaTeX package that does the formatting itself (usually with Biber as the backend), with better Unicode support, more entry types, and styles you can tweak in plain LaTeX. For a new thesis template, BibLaTeX is generally the easier choice, unless your school's template requires a .bst file.

Array: fixed size set at creation, can hold primitives or objects, uses [] and .length (e.g. int[] a = new int[5]; a[0]).

whats the difference between git merge and git rebase, short version pls

Merge combines two branches by creating a merge commit, so history keeps the branching shape and nothing is rewritten. Rebase replays your commits on top of another branch, giving a linear history but rewriting those commits with new hashes.

Rule of thumb: rebase your own local branches to tidy them, merge for shared branches, and never rebase commits others have already pulled.
ok and when would i use git pull --rebase

Use it when your local branch has commits that aren't pushed yet and the remote has new ones. Instead of making a merge commit, it fetches and replays your commits on top of the updated remote branch. That keeps history clean, and it's safe as long as your local commits haven't been pushed.

whats the actual difference between git merge and git rebase? my teammate on our robotics club repo keeps yelling at me to rebase

Merge combines two branches with a new merge commit, keeping history exactly as it happened. Rebase replays your commits on top of another branch, giving a linear history but rewriting your commits (new hashes).

Your teammate likely wants a clean history. Rule of thumb: rebase your own local feature branch onto main before opening a PR, but never rebase commits that others have already pulled, since that forces everyone to untangle the rewritten history.
ok so if i already pushed my branch is it still fine?

Fine if only you are using that branch. You'd need to push with `git push --force-with-lease` afterward, which is safer than plain --force because it refuses to overwrite commits you haven't seen. If anyone else has based work on the branch, coordinate with them first or just merge instead.

whats the difference between git merge and git rebase? my teammate on the discord bot keeps yelling at me for merging

Merge combines two branches by creating a new merge commit, preserving the full history exactly as it happened. Rebase replays your commits on top of another branch, producing a linear history but rewriting your commits (new hashes).

Rule of thumb: rebase your own local feature branch onto main to keep history clean, but never rebase commits that are already pushed and shared, since that forces everyone else to reconcile rewritten history. Merge is the safe choice for shared branches.
ok and how do I rebase my branch onto main

From your feature branch:

git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main

If there are conflicts, fix the files, then `git add <file>` and `git rebase --continue` (or `git rebase --abort` to back out). If you already pushed the branch, you'll need `git push --force-with-lease` afterward, so only do that if you're the only one working on it.

why does this keep remembering old items?

def add_item(item, items=[]):
    items.append(item)
    return items

print(add_item('a'))
print(add_item('b'))

The default list is created once, when the function is defined, not on each call. Every call without `items` reuses that same list, so the second call prints ['a', 'b'].

Fix it with None as the default:

def add_item(item, items=None):
    if items is None:
        items = []
    items.append(item)
    return items
ok does that happen with ints too

The default is still shared, but ints are immutable, so you can't change them in place. `n += 1` makes a new int and rebinds the local name, and the default stays the same. The bug only shows up with mutable defaults like lists, dicts and sets.

quick q, whats the difference between a p-value and a confidence interval? my stats prof explained it badly lol

A p-value is the probability of seeing data at least as extreme as yours if the null hypothesis were true. It answers "is this result surprising under no effect?" A confidence interval is a range of plausible values for the true effect size, built so that 95% of intervals made this way would contain the true value.

The p-value gives a yes/no style signal; the CI also shows how big and how precise the effect is. If a 95% CI for a difference excludes 0, the p-value is below 0.05.
ok so if the CI is like [0.1, 5.0] is that good

It excludes 0, so the result is statistically significant at the 0.05 level. But the range is wide: the true effect could be tiny (0.1) or fifty times larger (5.0). So the direction is fairly clear, but the size is imprecise, likely from a small sample or noisy data.

Here are a few options:

quick q for AP gov, whats the difference between a ceasefire and an armistice? my textbook is confusing

A ceasefire is a temporary halt to fighting, often local or short-term, and the war is still officially on. An armistice is a formal agreement to stop fighting more broadly and usually lasts until a peace treaty is negotiated. The Korean War is the classic example: the 1953 armistice stopped the fighting, but no peace treaty was ever signed, so the war is technically unresolved.

quick q, if I block out 45 min study sessions with 10 min breaks, how many full sessions fit between 4:00pm and 8:30pm?

quick q whats the difference between a primary and secondary source for my APUSH DBQ? like is a textbook secondary

Yes, a textbook is a secondary source.

A primary source is created during the time period you're studying, such as letters, speeches, laws, photos, or diaries. A secondary source is written later by someone analyzing that period, such as textbooks or historians' articles.

For the DBQ, the documents you're given are almost always primary sources, so focus on who wrote each one, when, and why. That's the sourcing you need for the HIPP analysis.

quick q for my lit review, whats the difference between a systematic review and a meta-analysis? my teacher keeps using them like theyre the same thing

They're related but not identical.

A systematic review is a structured way of finding and evaluating all the studies on a question. It uses a defined search strategy, clear inclusion and exclusion criteria, and a quality assessment. The results can be summarized in words.

A meta-analysis is a statistical technique that pools the numerical results from several studies into one combined estimate, such as an overall effect size. It usually sits inside a systematic review, but only when the studies are similar enough to combine.

So every meta-analysis should be based on a systematic review, but plenty of systematic reviews have no meta-analysis, because the studies are too different to pool.

messages.content:
Later School Start Times and Adolescent Outcomes: A Review of the Evidence
Halvorsen, M., & Ibekwe, T. (2025). Journal of Adolescent Sleep and Learning, 14(2), 88-121.
DOI: 10.5555/jasl.2025.0142
Published: March 2025 | Open access

ABSTRACT
This review synthesizes 31 studies (2008-2024) covering about 214,000 students in grades 8-12
across the US, Canada, and Europe. Schools that moved start times to 8:30 a.m. or later
generally saw longer sleep, fewer tardies, and modest gains in attendance. Effects on test
scores were smaller and less consistent.

1. BACKGROUND
Puberty delays circadian timing by roughly one to two hours. A 7:30 a.m. start
conflicts with this shift. Pediatric groups have recommended 8:30 a.m. or later since 2014.

2. METHODS
Databases searched: PubMed, ERIC, PsycINFO. Inclusion: pre/post or matched comparison design,
at least 6 months follow-up, objective or self-reported sleep measure.
Of 412 records screened, 31 met criteria. 19 were quasi-experimental, 9 were cohort, 3 were RCT-like.

3. KEY FINDINGS
Sleep: Students gained a mean of 34 minutes of weekday sleep (95% CI 27-41) after delays of 30-60 min.
Attendance: Average daily attendance rose 1.8 percentage points (range 0.4-3.9).
Tardiness: Late arrivals fell 23% in the 14 studies that measured them.
Grades: GPA change was +0.06 on a 4.0 scale (CI -0.01 to +0.13), not statistically significant.
Test scores: 8 of 12 studies found small gains in math and reading; effect size d = 0.08.
Mental health: Depressive symptom scores dropped 8% in 7 of 9 studies measuring them.
Car crashes: 3 studies of drivers 16-18 reported crash rates 14-16% lower after the change.

4. TABLE 1. SELECTED STUDIES
Study | Location | n | Shift | Main result
Alder 2012 | Minnesota, US | 9,000 | 7:25 to 8:30 | +45 min sleep
Brandt 2016 | Seattle, US | 180 | 7:50 to 8:45 | +34 min sleep, +4.5% grades
Cole 2018 | Ontario, CA | 5,400 | 8:00 to 8:50 | attendance +1.2 pts
Dufresne 2020 | Lyon, FR | 2,100 | 8:00 to 9:00 | tardies -31%
Eriksen 2022 | Oslo, NO | 3,300 | 8:15 to 9:00 | no GPA change
Foley 2023 | Georgia, US | 41,000 | 7:15 to 8:30 | crashes -16%

5. MODERATING FACTORS
Gains were larger when the delay was 45 minutes or more.
Gains shrank when after-school activities pushed bedtimes later.
Rural districts with long bus rides saw smaller sleep gains (+19 min).
Lower-income students showed the largest attendance improvements (+3.1 pts).

6. LIMITATIONS
Most studies lacked randomization. Self-reported sleep may be inflated.
Publication bias is possible; funnel plot shows mild asymmetry.
Few studies tracked outcomes beyond two years.
Cost and schedule effects on sports and jobs were rarely measured.

7. CONCLUSION
Later start times reliably improve sleep, attendance, and mood. Academic gains are small.
Districts should plan for transportation and activity scheduling.

HOW TO CITE
APA 7: Halvorsen, M., & Ibekwe, T. (2025). Later school start times and adolescent outcomes: A review of the evidence. Journal of Adolescent Sleep and Learning, 14(2), 88-121. https://doi.org/10.5555/jasl.2025.0142

This is a 2025 review of 31 studies (about 214,000 students, grades 8-12) on start times of 8:30 a.m. or later. Key stats for you:
- Sleep: +34 minutes on weekdays on average (95% CI 27-41)
- Attendance: +1.8 percentage points; tardies down 23%
- Mental health: depressive symptoms down 8% (7 of 9 studies)
- Crashes: 14-16% lower for drivers 16-18 (3 studies)
- Grades and tests: GPA +0.06 (not significant), test score effect size d = 0.08

It also says gains were larger with delays of 45+ minutes and smaller in rural districts (+19 min). For limitations, most studies lacked randomization, sleep was often self-reported, and few followed students beyond two years. Those are worth acknowledging in your paper.

APA 7 citation: Halvorsen, M., & Ibekwe, T. (2025). Later school start times and adolescent outcomes: A review of the evidence. Journal of Adolescent Sleep and Learning, 14(2), 88-121. https://doi.org/10.5555/jasl.2025.0142

whats the difference between a systematic review and a meta-analysis? writing a section for my research methods paper and keep mixing them up

A systematic review is a structured, reproducible method for finding, screening, and summarizing all the studies on a specific question. You define search terms, inclusion criteria, and quality checks up front, and the results can be summarized in words or tables.

A meta-analysis is a statistical technique that pools numerical results from multiple studies into one combined effect estimate. It is often part of a systematic review, but only when the studies are similar enough to combine.

So: every meta-analysis should be based on a systematic review, but not every systematic review includes a meta-analysis.

what's the difference between git merge and git rebase, like when would i actually use each

Merge combines two branches by creating a merge commit, keeping the full history exactly as it happened. Rebase replays your commits on top of another branch, producing a straight, linear history.

Use merge when integrating shared or public branches (like a PR into main), since it doesn't rewrite history. Use rebase to tidy up your own local feature branch or to pull in the latest main before opening a PR. Rule of thumb: never rebase commits others have already pulled.

COMMON APP ESSAY - DRAFT 3 FEEDBACK
From: Ms. Delgado

OVERALL
Strong, honest voice. The garage soldering opening is the best part.
Main issues: length, a confusing timeline, and a flat ending.

PARAGRAPH 1
Keep the hook as is.
Cut "Ever since I was little" - cliche.

PARAGRAPH 2
Timeline is confusing: "eighth grade" then "two years earlier".
Pick one anchor date and keep it.
The sentence about your dad's old radio is 54 words. Split it.

PARAGRAPH 3
What exactly broke when the radio first failed? Be specific.
Replace "it was a really hard problem" with the actual problem.
Good detail: the burnt-resistor smell. More like that.

PARAGRAPH 4
Too much tech name-dropping: Arduino, Raspberry Pi, ESP32, Python, Rust, Docker.
Pick two at most. Admissions readers skim lists.
This paragraph can lose about 60 words.

PARAGRAPH 5
The tutoring-club story is a different essay. Cut it or tie it to the radio.
Cutting it saves about 70 words.

CONCLUSION
Ending ("I learned that failure is a teacher") is generic.
Return to the garage image instead. Show the realization, do not state it.

GRAMMAR / STYLE
Line 12: "its" vs "it's".
Line 27: comma splice.
Paragraph 3: tense shifts from past to present.
Avoid "very" and "really" (7 uses).

NEXT STEPS
Send me Draft 4 by Tuesday 2026-12-29.
Target 640-650 words.
Do not submit until I've seen Draft 4.
Common App submission deadline you mentioned: 2027-01-01.

- Length: you're at 742 words and need 650 or fewer. Cut the tutoring-club paragraph (~70 words) and trim the tech list in paragraph 4 (~60 words) down to two tools.

- Small stuff: its/it's, a comma splice, tense shifts in paragraph 3, and 7 uses of "very" or "really".

Draft 4 is due to her Tuesday, Dec 29, and she wants to see it before you submit by Jan 1.

3 of 41 tests fail, and they're 3 separate bugs:
1. test_parse_menu_handles_empty_day: menu_parser.py:31 calls find_all on the result of select_one("table.menu"), which is None on an empty day. It needs a None check that returns an empty list.
2. test_parse_menu_euro_prices: the price comes back as None for the "Soup of the day" fixture. The parser probably doesn't handle a comma decimal like 3,50.
3. test_storage_roundtrip_votes: storage.py:77 inserts into a voted_at column that doesn't exist in the test DB, so a migration is likely missing or not applied.

The 4 utcnow() deprecation warnings in scheduler.py (lines 22, 58, 91) are not failures, but are worth swapping for datetime.now(datetime.UTC).

how do i cite an arxiv preprint in APA 7? need it for my methods section

function.name: web_search
function.arguments: {"query": "APA 7 citation format arXiv preprint reference list example", "num_results": 3}

messages.name: web_search
messages.content: [{"title":"Preprint and Unpublished Work Citations (APA 7th)","url":"https://writing.example.edu/apa7/preprints","snippet":"Format: Author, A. A. (Year). Title of work. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/xxxx.xxxxx — Give the repository name as the publisher. If the preprint is later published in a journal, cite the journal version instead."},{"title":"APA Style Quick Guide: Reference Examples","url":"https://styleguide.example.org/apa/references","snippet":"In-text: (Author, Year). Italicize the title of a preprint as a standalone work. Include the arXiv identifier in the URL."},{"title":"Citing preprints - library FAQ","url":"https://library.example.net/faq/preprints","snippet":"Check whether a peer-reviewed version exists before citing the preprint."}]

APA 7 format for an arXiv preprint:

Author, A. A., & Author, B. B. (Year). *Title of the work*. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/xxxx.xxxxx

The in-text citation is (Author & Author, Year). The title is italicized, and the repository name (arXiv) goes where the publisher normally would. If a peer-reviewed version has since been published, cite that one instead. This comes from the sources found at writing.example.edu and styleguide.example.org.

messages.content:
Harlow Valley Community Scholarship 2027

About the award
The Harlow Valley Community Foundation awards ten scholarships of $2,500
each to graduating high school seniors who plan to attend a two- or
four-year college in the fall of 2027. Awards are paid directly to the
school and may be renewed once with a 3.0 GPA.

Who can apply
- Current high school seniors living in Harlow County
- Minimum unweighted GPA of 3.2
- At least 40 hours of documented community service
- Planning to enroll full-time in fall 2027

What to submit
1. Online application form (name, school, GPA, intended major)
2. Official or unofficial transcript (PDF)
3. One letter of recommendation from a teacher, counselor, or
   community leader. Family members are not accepted.
4. Service log signed by a supervisor or organization contact
5. Personal essay (see below)

Essay prompt
Describe a problem in your community that you have tried to help solve.
What did you do, what did you learn, and how will you carry that
forward in college?

Essay requirements
- Maximum 650 words, minimum 400 words
- Double spaced, 12 pt font if uploading a document
- Upload as PDF or paste into the form
- Do not include your name in the essay body; use your applicant ID
  instead (you receive it after submitting the form)
- Essays that exceed the word limit will not be read

Important dates
- Applications open: December 1, 2026
- Recommendation letters due: February 5, 2027
- Application and essay deadline: February 15, 2027, 11:59 PM Eastern
- Finalists notified: March 20, 2027
- Interviews (finalists only): April 3-4, 2027
- Winners announced: April 25, 2027

Selection criteria
Applications are scored on community impact (40%), essay quality
(30%), service hours (20%), and academic record (10%).

Frequently asked questions
Q: Can I apply to more than one foundation scholarship?
A: Students may only win one Harlow Valley award.

Q: Can my recommender email the letter directly?
A: Yes. Recommenders can email letters to recommend@example.org
   with the applicant's name and school in the subject line.

Q: Do I need to be a US citizen?
A: No. Residents of Harlow County are eligible regardless of
   citizenship status.

Q: Can I edit my application after submitting?
A: Edits are allowed until the deadline using your applicant ID.

Contact
Harlow Valley Community Foundation
Email: scholarships@example.org
Office hours: Monday to Thursday, 9 AM to 4 PM

Here's what the Harlow Valley scholarship ($2,500, ten awards) needs. The deadline is Feb 15, 2027 at 11:59 PM Eastern.

Submit:
- Online application form
- Transcript (PDF)
- One recommendation letter from a teacher, counselor, or community leader (no family). It's due earlier, Feb 5, and can be emailed to recommend@example.org.
- Service log signed by a supervisor (40+ hours required)
- Essay

Essay: 400 to 650 words (over 650 won't be read), on a community problem you've tried to help solve, what you did and learned, and how you'll carry it into college. Leave your name out and use your applicant ID instead. You also need a 3.2 unweighted GPA, and community impact is 40% of the score.

Finalists are notified March 20 and winners announced April 25.

i'm writing my research paper on school start times. can you pull https://example.org/reviews/later-start-times-14-studies and give me the main findings + limitations i can cite

messages.name: fetch_url
messages.content:
Later School Start Times and Adolescent Outcomes: A Review of 14 Studies
Okafor, M., Brandt, L., & Teixeira, S. (2025). Journal of Applied Adolescent Health, 18(2), 101-124.

ABSTRACT
We reviewed 14 studies published between 2009 and 2024 that examined schools shifting start times 25 to 85 minutes later. Across 61,380 students in grades 6-12, later starts were associated with more sleep, modestly better attendance, fewer teen driving crashes, and lower reported depressive symptoms. Effects on grades were small.

1. BACKGROUND
Adolescent circadian rhythms shift later during puberty, making early bedtimes biologically difficult. Many districts begin classes before 8:00 AM. Professional pediatric groups have recommended start times of 8:30 AM or later for middle and high schools.

2. METHODS
We searched four databases for studies reporting a before/after or matched-comparison design. Studies were included if at least one outcome was measured for 6 months or more. Of the 14 studies, 3 used quasi-experimental designs with comparison districts and 11 used before/after designs without a control group. Countries represented: United States (9), Canada (2), Norway (1), Australia (1), Japan (1).

3. RESULTS
3.1 Sleep
All 14 studies measured sleep. Students gained between 25 and 77 minutes of sleep on school nights, with a median gain of 43 minutes. Weekend sleep differences narrowed in 8 of the 10 studies that reported them.

3.2 Attendance and tardiness
Nine studies reported attendance. Average attendance rose 1.9 percentage points (range 0.4 to 3.6). Tardiness fell in 7 of 8 studies measuring it.

3.3 Academic performance
Seven studies reported grades or test scores. The pooled effect was small (d = 0.08, 95% CI -0.01 to 0.17) and not statistically significant. Gains were largest in core subjects taught in the first period.

3.4 Driving safety
Three studies, all in the United States, examined crash data for drivers aged 16-18. Crash rates fell between 12% and 16% after start times moved later.

3.5 Mental health
Six studies measured depressive symptoms through self-report. Five found lower scores after the shift. One found no change. None measured clinical diagnosis.

3.6 Athletics and extracurriculars
Two studies noted later practice times and dismissal. Neither found a drop in participation, but both reported scheduling complaints from coaches.

4. COSTS AND IMPLEMENTATION
Four studies discussed busing. Districts that staggered bus routes reported added transportation costs in 3 of the 4 cases. One district reported savings after consolidating routes. Community surveys showed initial opposition that declined after one year in 5 of 6 districts surveyed.

5. LIMITATIONS
- Only 3 of 14 studies had a comparison group, so changes may reflect other trends.
- Sleep was self-reported in 11 studies.
- Ten studies followed students for less than 2 years, so long-term effects are unknown.
- Funnel plot asymmetry suggests possible publication bias toward positive results.
- Most samples came from suburban districts; rural and low-income schools are underrepresented.

6. CONCLUSION
The evidence supports modest but consistent benefits for sleep, attendance, driving safety, and mood. Benefits to academic performance remain uncertain. Stronger controlled studies with objective sleep measures are needed.

Funding: None declared. Conflicts of interest: None declared.
Keywords: school start time, adolescent sleep, circadian rhythm, attendance, crash rates

Source: Okafor, Brandt & Teixeira (2025), Journal of Applied Adolescent Health, 18(2), 101-124. It reviews 14 studies (2009-2024, N = 61,380) of start times moved 25-85 minutes later.

Main findings:
- Sleep: +25 to +77 minutes per school night (median +43), measured in all 14 studies.
- Attendance: +1.9 percentage points on average (9 studies); tardiness fell in 7 of 8.
- Driving: teen crash rates fell 12-16% (3 US studies).
- Mood: depressive symptoms were lower in 5 of 6 studies.
- Grades: small, non-significant effect (d = 0.08, CI -0.01 to 0.17).

Limitations to mention: only 3 of 14 studies had a comparison group, sleep was mostly self-reported (11 studies), 10 studies followed students for under 2 years, possible publication bias, and rural and low-income schools are underrepresented. Busing costs also rose in 3 of the 4 districts that discussed them.

quick q, whats the difference between `git merge --squash` and a regular merge? my teammate on the discord bot repo keeps asking me to squash and idk why

A regular merge keeps every commit from your branch and usually adds a merge commit, so the full history of the branch shows up on main. `git merge --squash` takes all the changes from your branch and stages them as one set of changes. You then make a single commit yourself, and no link to the original branch commits is kept.

Your teammate likely wants squashing to keep main's history clean: one commit per feature instead of lots of "fix typo" and "wip" commits. The downside is that you lose the detailed history, and the branch will look unmerged to git, so delete it afterward.
ok makes sense. so after squash I just git commit and then delete the branch with -D?

Yes. After `git merge --squash feature-branch`, run `git commit -m "Add slash command cooldowns"`. Git doesn't see the branch as merged, so `git branch -d` will refuse. Use `git branch -D feature-branch`, and only after confirming the squash commit is on main, since -D deletes without checking.

whats the difference between a systematic review and a meta-analysis? need it for my psych AP research project

messages.name: web_search
messages.content: [{"title":"Systematic Reviews vs Meta-Analyses - Example University Library","url":"https://library.example.edu/guides/reviews","snippet":"A systematic review uses a structured, reproducible method to find and appraise all studies on a question. A meta-analysis is a statistical technique that combines numerical results from multiple studies."},{"title":"Types of Reviews","url":"https://research.example.org/review-types","snippet":"Many systematic reviews include a meta-analysis, but not all do; a meta-analysis requires studies similar enough to pool statistically."}]

A systematic review is a structured, reproducible way of finding and evaluating all the studies on a question. A meta-analysis is the statistical step of pooling numerical results from multiple studies. Many systematic reviews include a meta-analysis, but only when the studies are similar enough to combine. Source: library.example.edu/guides/reviews.

why does `[1,2,3].map(parseInt)` return [1, NaN, NaN] in js lol

`map` passes three arguments to the callback: value, index, and array. `parseInt` takes (string, radix), so it receives the index as the radix:

- parseInt(1, 0) -> radix 0 is treated as 10, so 1
- parseInt(2, 1) -> radix 1 is invalid, so NaN
- parseInt(3, 2) -> 3 isn't a valid binary digit, so NaN

Fix it with `[1,2,3].map(n => parseInt(n, 10))` or just `.map(Number)`.

quick check: p = 0.04 means theres a 4% chance the null hypothesis is true right?

No, that's a common misreading. A p-value of 0.04 means that if the null hypothesis were true, you'd see data at least this extreme about 4% of the time. It isn't the probability that the null is true. That would need a prior and a Bayesian analysis.
ok can you rephrase this for my paper: 'The result was significant so the hypothesis is probably right.'

Try: "The result was statistically significant (p = 0.04), which provides evidence against the null hypothesis and is consistent with our proposed hypothesis." It avoids claiming the hypothesis is proven or probably true.

whats the difference between SQLite WAL mode and the default rollback journal? need it for my project writeup, link a good source pls

function.name: web_search
function.arguments: {"query": "SQLite WAL mode vs rollback journal differences", "num_results": 4}

messages.name: web_search
messages.content: [{"title":"Write-Ahead Logging - SQLite","url":"https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html","snippet":"WAL provides more concurrency as readers do not block writers and a writer does not block readers. WAL is significantly faster in most scenarios."},{"title":"Atomic Commit In SQLite","url":"https://www.sqlite.org/atomiccommit.html","snippet":"How SQLite implements atomic commit using a rollback journal."},{"title":"SQLite WAL explained - example.org dev blog","url":"https://blog.example.org/sqlite-wal-explained","snippet":"Changes are appended to a separate -wal file and later checkpointed into the main database."}]

In the default rollback journal, the original pages are copied to a journal before changes are written to the database file, and readers and writers block each other. WAL mode instead appends changes to a separate -wal file that is later checkpointed into the main database, so readers don't block the writer and vice versa, and it's usually faster. Best source for your writeup is the official page: https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html, and https://www.sqlite.org/atomiccommit.html covers the rollback journal side.

why does [1, 2, 10, 21].sort() in JS give me [1, 10, 2, 21] lol

Array.prototype.sort() with no comparator converts items to strings and compares them lexicographically, so "10" comes before "2" (since "1" < "2"). Pass a comparator for numeric order: `[1, 2, 10, 21].sort((a, b) => a - b)`.
does that mutate the original array? i need to keep it

Yes, sort() sorts in place and returns the same array. To keep the original, copy first: `[...arr].sort((a, b) => a - b)`, or use `arr.toSorted((a, b) => a - b)`, which returns a new array (Node 20+ and current browsers).

whats the difference between a primary and secondary source? need it for my history paper citations

A primary source is firsthand evidence from the time period you're studying, such as letters, diaries, speeches, photos, official records, or original data. A secondary source analyzes or interprets primary sources after the fact, such as textbooks, journal articles, and biographies. For your paper, cite primary sources as your evidence and use secondary sources for context and to show what historians argue.

quick q, how do i cite a github repo in APA 7 for my research project? no author listed just the org

Use the organization as the author, then the year, the repo name in italics with the type in brackets, and the URL:

OrgName. (Year). *Repo-name* [Computer software]. GitHub. https://github.com/orgname/repo-name

For example: Example Labs. (2024). *fastgraph* [Computer software]. GitHub. https://github.com/example-labs/fastgraph

Use the year of the release you used, or the latest commit year if there are no releases. The in-text citation is (Example Labs, 2024). If the organization is also the publisher, GitHub still goes in the publisher spot.

messages.content:
# Feedback on 'The Tide Chart' - personal statement, draft 3
Reviewed: 2027-01-04
Target: Westbrook Coastal Scholarship, 650 words max, due Jan 15
Current length: 721 words

## Mr. Alvarez (English)
- Opening image of your grandfather's tide chart is the best thing in the essay. Keep it.
- Para 2 (ferry job) is 140 words of telling. Cut to ~70 and add one concrete scene, e.g. the morning the engine stalled.
- 'I learned the value of hard work' is a cliche. Say what actually changed in you.
- Para 3 has three 'was' sentences in a row. Vary the rhythm.
- Dialogue with the harbormaster is flat; sharpen it or cut it.
- Conclusion repeats the intro almost word for word. Try ending on the scholarship goal (marine biology) instead.
- Watch passive voice: 'it was decided that' (para 3), 'mistakes were made' (para 4).
- Typo: 'tide' vs 'tied' in sentence 2 of para 4.

## Tessa (peer)
- Loved the grandfather part, made me tear up a little.
- Wanted to know more about why you want marine biology; it shows up only in the last line.
- The sentence starting 'Throughout my life' can go.
- Para 4 is great, don't cut it.
- Maybe name the ferry? Specifics make it real.

## Jonah (peer)
- Opening is confusing, I didn't know the chart was a paper one until para 2. Maybe start with the ferry instead.
- Timeline jumps from age 9 to age 15 to age 12 in para 3.
- Too many numbers (tide heights) in para 1, cut two of them.
- Like the ending line about 'reading the water'.
- Para 2 drags.

## Writing center (Ms. Ibarra, 2027-01-05)
- Strong voice overall.
- Word count must be cut by at least 71 words; do not go over 650 even by a few.
- Check the scholarship portal: it wants the essay pasted as plain text, no italics.
- Bring final draft by Friday Jan 9 for one last read.
- Don't over-polish; the roughness in para 4 is a strength.

## Running to-do (compiled)
[ ] Cut para 2 to ~70 words and add one scene
[ ] Replace hard work cliche
[ ] Fix timeline order in para 3
[ ] Rewrite conclusion
[ ] Fix passive voice (para 3, 4)
[ ] Fix tide/tied typo
[ ] Add why-marine-biology earlier
[ ] Trim 71+ words total
[ ] Remove 'Throughout my life' sentence (undecided)
[ ] Writing center final read by Jan 9
[ ] Submit by Jan 15

Everyone likes the grandfather's tide chart and para 4, so keep those. The main problems:
- Length: you're at 721 words and the limit is 650, so cut at least 71.
- Para 2 (ferry job) is 140 words of telling; Alvarez and Jonah both say it drags. Cut it to about 70 and add one scene.
- The 'hard work' line is a cliche, and the conclusion repeats the intro. End on marine biology instead, and mention it earlier (Tessa's point).
- Para 3 has a jumbled timeline (ages 9, 15, 12) and some passive voice.
- One disagreement: Jonah finds the opening confusing and wants to start with the ferry, but Alvarez says keep it. Clarifying early that the chart is a paper one might fix both.

Start with the para 2 cut, since it also solves most of the word count. Bring the final draft to Ms. Ibarra by Fri Jan 9; the due date is Jan 15.

messages.name: fetch_url
messages.content:
Reference Managers for Students: 2027 Comparison
Updated May 2027 by the Example Library Guides team

Why use a reference manager?
A reference manager stores your sources, formats citations, and builds a bibliography automatically.
This guide compares four popular tools for high school and undergraduate work.
We tested each with a 25-source research paper in MLA 9 and APA 7.

SHELFREF
Price: Free, open source.
Storage: 300 MB free cloud sync; paid plans from $20/year for 2 GB.
Google Docs: Official add-on, works well, inserts in-text citations and bibliography.
Word processors: Also supports Word and LibreOffice.
Browser capture: Excellent. One click saves articles, PDFs and metadata.
Styles: 10,000+ citation styles including MLA 9 and APA 7.
Offline: Full desktop app works offline.
Learning curve: Moderate; about 30 minutes to get comfortable.

CITENEST
Price: Free tier; Pro $5/month (student discount $3/month).
Storage: 2 GB free.
Google Docs: Add-on is functional but slow with 50+ sources.
Browser capture: Good, sometimes misses author names on news sites.
Styles: MLA, APA, Chicago, and about 1,500 others.
Offline: Limited; mobile app is offline-capable, web app is not.
Collaboration: Shared libraries are free for up to 3 people.
Learning curve: Low. Easiest interface in our test.

PAPERLANE
Price: $4/month, no permanent free tier (14-day trial).
Storage: Unlimited PDFs.
Google Docs: Best integration of the four, live bibliography updates.
Browser capture: Very good.
Styles: Around 2,000 styles.
Offline: None. Web only.
Annotations: Strong PDF highlighting and notes that sync across devices.
Learning curve: Low.

BIBBOX
Price: Free for individuals.
Storage: 100 MB, no paid upgrade.
Google Docs: No add-on; export a bibliography file and paste it in.
Browser capture: Basic. Often needs manual cleanup.
Styles: MLA, APA, Chicago, Harvard only.
Offline: Yes.
Learning curve: Very low.

ACCURACY TEST (25 sources)
ShelfRef: 2 errors (both missing DOI on older articles).
CiteNest: 5 errors (author names, italics in titles).
Paperlane: 3 errors.
BibBox: 8 errors.

OUR RECOMMENDATIONS
Best free overall: ShelfRef.
Best for ease of use: CiteNest.
Best for Google Docs power users: Paperlane (paid).
Best for quick one-off papers: BibBox.
Note: Always check generated citations against the style manual before submitting.

End of guide.

For a Google Docs paper with 25-ish sources, ShelfRef looks like the best fit. It's free, has an official Google Docs add-on, the most accurate citations in the test (2 errors out of 25, both missing DOIs), and it supports MLA 9 and APA 7. The downsides are 300 MB of free sync and about 30 minutes to learn. CiteNest is easier to use, but its Docs add-on slows down past 50 sources and it made 5 errors. Paperlane has the best Docs integration but costs $4/month, and BibBox has no Docs add-on. Whichever you pick, check the generated citations against the style manual.

whats the difference between a systematic review and a meta-analysis? doing a lit review for my bio research class

A systematic review collects and critically appraises all studies on a question using a predefined, reproducible search and inclusion method, then summarizes the findings, usually in words and tables. A meta-analysis is a statistical step that pools numerical results from multiple studies into one combined effect estimate.

Many systematic reviews include a meta-analysis, but not all do. If the studies are too different in design or measurement to combine, the review stays narrative. A meta-analysis without a systematic search is weaker, since it may be biased toward whichever studies you happened to find.
ok so for a class lit review which one am i writing

Most likely neither in the strict sense. A class literature review is usually a narrative review: you pick and synthesize relevant papers without the full protocol or statistics. You can borrow from systematic reviews by stating your search terms, databases and inclusion criteria in a short methods paragraph. That makes it more credible, and your teacher may appreciate it.

quick q for my AP CS review, whats the difference between a stack and a queue? and when would u use each

A stack is last-in, first-out (LIFO): you push and pop from the same end. A queue is first-in, first-out (FIFO): you add at the back and remove from the front.

Use a stack for things like undo history, function call tracking, recursion, or matching parentheses. Use a queue for things like task scheduling, print jobs, or breadth-first search.
ok and which one does DFS use
DFS uses a stack, either an explicit one or the call stack when you write it recursively. BFS is the one that uses a queue.

whats the apa 7 format for a journal article with 4 authors, i always forget the et al rule

In the reference list, APA 7 lists every author (up to 20), like this:

Last, F. M., Last, F. M., Last, F. M., & Last, F. M. (Year). Title of article in sentence case. *Journal Name in Title Case*, *volume*(issue), pages. https://doi.org/xxxx

In-text, use "et al." from the first citation when there are 3 or more authors: (Okafor et al., 2024). Only 1 or 2 authors get named every time.
ok and a website page with no author?

The title moves into the author spot:

*Title of page in italics*. (Year, Month Day). Site Name. URL

If the site name is the same as the author, you skip it. In-text, use a shortened title in italics for a standalone page: (*Reef Restoration Basics*, 2025). If there's no date, write (n.d.).

quick q, whats the difference between a p-value and a confidence interval? doing a stats lit review and want to explain it right

A p-value is the probability of seeing data at least as extreme as yours if the null hypothesis were true. It answers "is this result surprising under no effect?" and says nothing about how big the effect is.

A confidence interval is a range of plausible values for the effect size, built so that a 95% CI procedure captures the true value in about 95% of repeated studies. It shows both the size and the precision of the estimate.

They're linked: if a 95% CI excludes the null value (e.g., 0), then p < 0.05. For a lit review, CIs are usually more informative, so report both when the papers do.

messages.name: read_file
messages.content:
LAKEVIEW HIGH SCHOOL - COUNSELING OFFICE
Senior Newsletter - April 2027

Hello seniors! Here is everything happening this month.

== COLLEGE DECISIONS ==
Most regular-decision results are released by April 1. Check your portals.
Reply deadline for nearly all colleges is Saturday, May 1 (National Decision Day).
Submit your intent-to-enroll deposit directly to the college, not to us.
Waitlisted? Meet with your counselor by April 14 to plan a letter of continued interest.
Report your final decision through the Naviance "Where I'm Going" survey by April 30.

== FINANCIAL AID & SCHOLARSHIPS ==
Compare award letters using the worksheet in the counseling office (Room 112).
Lakeview Alumni Scholarship: application due Friday, April 9, 4:00 PM. Essay 500 words max.
Rotary Service Award: due April 16. Requires 2 letters of recommendation.
Counselors need 10 school days' notice for recommendation letters.
FAFSA corrections: deadlines vary by state; check with your college's aid office.
Local business scholarships are listed on the board outside Room 112.

== AP EXAMS ==
AP exams run May 3 - May 14 in the gym and library.
Order changes or cancellations must be made by April 16 to avoid a $40 unused-exam fee.
The exam schedule is posted on the main hallway board and the school website.
Bring: two No. 2 pencils, black pens, approved calculator, photo ID.
No phones or smartwatches in the testing room.
AP Art portfolio submissions are due April 30.
Students with testing accommodations should confirm room assignments with Ms. Delacroix.

== SENIOR ACTIVITIES ==
Yearbook senior quotes: due Monday, April 5 to Ms. Okafor in Room 208. Baby photos same date.
Cap and gown orders: due Thursday, April 8 at the bookstore window. $38. Late orders cannot be guaranteed.
Prom: Saturday, April 24, 7-11 PM, Harbor Convention Center.
Prom tickets are $45 until April 12, $60 after that.
Prom guest forms are due April 12 at the front office.
Senior Picnic: Friday, May 21, at Maple Grove Park.
Senior Awards Night: Tuesday, May 25, 6:30 PM, auditorium.
Graduation: Saturday, June 12, 10:00 AM, Lakeview Stadium.
Graduation rehearsal: Thursday, June 10, 9:00 AM, attendance required.

== GRADUATION REQUIREMENTS ==
Seniors with an incomplete credit must meet with a counselor by April 9.
Community service: all 40 hours must be logged by May 7. Forms go to Mr. Brandt.
Senior project presentations: May 10-14. Sign up for a slot by April 19.
Library books and textbooks must be returned by May 28.
Unpaid fines will hold your diploma.

== MISC ==
Final transcript requests open May 17 through Parchment.
Parking permits for the last quarter are free at the front office.
Lost and found will be cleared out on April 30.
Questions? Stop by Room 112 or email counseling@lakeview.example.edu.

Here are the deadlines in date order:
- Apr 5: yearbook senior quote and baby photo to Ms. Okafor (Rm 208)
- Apr 8: cap and gown order ($38, bookstore window)
- Apr 9: Alumni Scholarship application (4 PM, 500-word essay), and a counselor meeting if you have an incomplete credit
- Apr 12: prom guest form, and prom tickets go from $45 to $60 after this
- Apr 14: counselor meeting if you're waitlisted
- Apr 16: Rotary Award (needs 2 recommendation letters, and counselors want 10 school days' notice), and AP order changes or cancellations to avoid the $40 fee
- Apr 19: sign up for a senior project slot
- Apr 30: Naviance decision survey
- May 1: college decision and deposit

After that: community service hours are due May 7 (40 total), AP exams run May 3-14, and graduation is June 12 with required rehearsal on June 10.

whats the actual difference between bibtex and biblatex, need to know for my research paper formatting

messages.name: web_search
messages.content: [{"title":"BibTeX vs BibLaTeX - Example TeX Guide","url":"https://example.org/tex/bibtex-vs-biblatex","snippet":"BibTeX is the older bibliography processor with styles written in .bst files. BibLaTeX handles formatting in LaTeX macros, supports Unicode, and is processed with Biber."},{"title":"Which bibliography tool should I use?","url":"https://example.net/latex-faq/bibliography","snippet":"BibLaTeX offers more entry types, easier customization of citation styles, and better support for non-English sources. BibTeX is still required by some journals."}]

BibTeX is the older system and uses .bst style files, while BibLaTeX does the formatting in LaTeX itself, runs with Biber, supports Unicode, and makes custom citation styles much easier. Use BibLaTeX unless your teacher or journal specifically requires BibTeX.

Units follow the College Board CED, 5 units total.

- Textbook: American Government (OpenStax), free PDF on class site

Tests 40% / Free-response & essays 25% / Quizzes 15% / Homework 10% / Participation 10%

Phones go in the caddy at the start of class.

ap calc q: whats d/dx of x^2 * ln(x)? is x(2ln x + 1) an ok final answer
Use the product rule: d/dx[x² ln x] = 2x·ln x + x²·(1/x) = 2x ln x + x. Factored, that's x(2 ln x + 1). Yes, that's a fine final answer; no need to expand or simplify further.

quick q, if my electric bill is $84.50 and I split it 3 ways but my roommate only pays for 2 days of the 30 day month, what's fair

One fair way is to split by person-days. Total person-days: 2 people x 30 + 1 person x 2 = 62. Each person-day costs $84.50 / 62 ≈ $1.36.

- Each full-month person: 30 x $1.36 ≈ $40.89
- The 2-day roommate: 2 x $1.36 ≈ $2.73

That totals $84.51 with rounding. If you'd rather keep it simple, a 3-way split would be $28.17 each, but that overcharges the short-stay roommate.

whats the difference between git merge and git rebase, like when would i actually pick one. working on a branch w/ a friend on our discord bot

Merge combines two branches with a merge commit, keeping history exactly as it happened. Rebase replays your commits on top of another branch, giving a straight, linear history but rewriting those commits.

For you and a friend sharing a branch:
- Use merge to bring main into the shared branch. It's safe and doesn't rewrite anything.
- Use rebase only on your own local, unpushed commits (e.g. `git pull --rebase` to tidy up before pushing).

Rule of thumb: never rebase commits that others have already pulled, since it changes their hashes and causes conflicts.

whats the difference between git merge and git rebase, like when would i actually use each one

Merge combines two branches by creating a merge commit, preserving the full history as it happened. Rebase replays your commits on top of another branch, giving a clean linear history but rewriting your commits.

messages.content:
FEEDBACK ON: "The Ticking Room" - Common App draft 3
Word count: 712 (limit 650)
Collected: 2026-10-04

== Ms. Penhallow (English) ==
1. Paragraph 1: three sentences of throat-clearing before the shop appears. Open at the moment you pry the back off the pocket watch.
2. The watch-repair scene (para 3) is the best writing in the piece. Slow down there; add one sensory detail, not three.
3. "Time teaches patience" is a told lesson. Let the scene show it.
4. You switch between past and present tense in paragraphs 2 and 4. Pick past.
5. Cut "journey" (3 uses) and "passion" (2 uses).
6. Final paragraph reaches for a big statement about the future. Return to the bench and the loupe instead.
7. Grandfather's dialogue is great. Keep "Never force a spring."
8. You need to cut about 65 words. Paragraph 2 (family history) can lose half.
9. Check that the shop's name is spelled the same way throughout (Oakhurst & Son vs Oakhurst and Son).

== Maya (peer) ==
1. I got lost in paragraph 2, too many relatives.
2. Love the smell-of-oil detail in paragraph 3.
3. Who is the audience? Admissions readers do not know what a balance wheel is. One quick explanation, please.
4. The sentence "I realized I was more than just a student" feels generic.
5. Title is good, keep it.
6. Transition from para 3 to 4 is abrupt. Add one linking sentence.
7. Ending feels like every other essay about grandparents.
8. Typo: "escapment" should be "escapement" (para 3).
9. Typo: "it's" should be "its" in the last paragraph.

== Jonas (peer) ==
1. First line is slow, I almost stopped reading.
2. Para 4 mentions your coding projects, which seems unrelated. Either connect it to repairing watches (debugging = diagnosing?) or cut it.
3. I actually like the debugging idea, make it explicit but short.
4. Too many adjectives in para 1.
5. The part where your grandfather's hands shake is moving. Do not explain it.
6. Cut the sentence about winning the regional robotics event; it is not what this essay is about.
7. Ending could echo the opening image.
8. Overall: strong voice, needs trimming.

== Ms. Penhallow: priority order ==
A. Cut to 650 words (hard limit in the portal).
B. Rewrite the opening to start in the scene.
C. Fix tense, typos, and the shop name spelling.
D. Decide on the coding paragraph: connect or cut.
E. Rewrite the ending to return to the bench.
F. Add one-line explanation of the balance wheel/escapement.

Next check-in: draft 4 to Ms. Penhallow by Tue Oct 13.
Early Action deadline: Nov 1.

Fix the length first: you're at 712 words against a 650 limit, so cut about 65, mostly from the family-history paragraph 2. Next, rewrite the opening to start at the moment you open the watch, then fix the tense switches (paragraphs 2 and 4), the "escapment" and "it's/its" typos, and the inconsistent "Oakhurst & Son" spelling.

Three content decisions remain. Either connect the coding paragraph to watch repair (debugging as diagnosing) or cut it. Give the ending a return to the bench instead of a big future statement. Add a one-line explanation of the balance wheel. Everyone agrees the repair scene and "Never force a spring" are strong, so keep them. Ms. Penhallow wants draft 4 by Tue Oct 13.

- Opening line about burning my thumb on the first circuit board is strong. Keep it.

- Transition into the robotics club paragraph is abrupt.
- Paragraph 3 has too many semicolons.

- Ending is a cliche ('this journey taught me').
- Total at 648/650, so any additions need equal cuts.

## Priya (peer) - 2026-11-01
- Loved the radio scene. Felt like I was in the garage.
- Robotics paragraph reads like a resume. Pick one moment, not four competitions.
- 'Passionate about engineering' appears twice. Cut both.
- Last paragraph mentions Halvorsen's course catalog; feels tacked on.
- Typo: 'recieved' in paragraph 4.

## Mr. Alvarez (counselor) - 2026-11-03
- Essay needs to show who you are beyond the robotics team; activities list already covers that.
- Suggest connecting the radio repair to why you build tools for other people (tutoring-scheduler app).
- 'I am the best programmer on my team' sounds arrogant. Rephrase.
- ED deadline reminder: Halvorsen University ED closes 2026-11-15, 11:59 pm.
- Confirm teacher rec submissions before Nov 12.

## Dad - 2026-11-05
- Could mention that Grandpa Hiro taught you to read a schematic.
- Likes the ending actually.
- Thinks the title is too gimmicky.

## Changes made
- [x] Fixed semicolons in paragraph 3 (v3)
- [x] Fixed 'recieved' typo (v4)
- [x] Removed 'passionate about engineering' x2 (v4)
- [x] Removed 'I learned a lot about perseverance' (v4)
- [ ] Rewrite ending
- [ ] Cut robotics paragraph to one moment
- [ ] Expand radio scene (needs cuts elsewhere)
- [ ] Rephrase 'best programmer' line
- [ ] Fix transition into robotics paragraph
- [ ] Decide on title

## Notes
- Brandt and Priya both flagged the robotics paragraph; highest priority.
- Alvarez wants radio -> tutoring-scheduler link; this could replace the ending.
- Final read by Ms. Brandt requested by Nov 12.

Smaller leftovers are rephrasing the 'best programmer' line, smoothing the transition, and picking a title. Timeline: Ms. Brandt's final read by Nov 12, and ED closes Nov 15 at 11:59 pm, so 6 days from today.

messages.name: fetch_url
messages.content:
PM2.5 Sensor Comparison for Student and DIY Projects
Updated: 2026-08-14 | Author: Dana Whitcombe, Open Air Lab

OVERVIEW
We ran three low-cost laser particle sensors next to a reference-grade monitor for 30 days
(July 2026) on a covered balcony in a mid-sized city. Readings were logged every 60 seconds.
All sensors were powered by the same 5 V supply and polled over their native interface.
Humidity ranged from 38% to 94% during the test.

TEST SETUP
- Reference: BAM-style monitor on loan from a county lab
- Placement: 1.5 m apart, same height, shielded from rain
- Calibration: none applied; factory settings only
- Metric: R-squared of 1-hour averages vs. reference, plus mean absolute error (MAE) in ug/m3

SENSOR 1: NIMBUS PM-3 ($14)
- Interface: UART, 3.3 V logic
- R-squared: 0.71 overall; 0.52 when humidity > 85%
- MAE: 6.8 ug/m3
- Power: 100 mA while running
- Rated life: ~12,000 hours (vendor claim)
- Notes: Overreads in fog. Library support is good (Arduino and MicroPython).
  No datasheet revision since 2022.
- Verdict: fine for classroom demos, weak for anything you want to publish.

SENSOR 2: AEROSENSE S5 ($29)
- Interface: I2C and UART
- R-squared: 0.86 overall; 0.74 when humidity > 85%
- MAE: 3.9 ug/m3
- Power: 70 mA
- Rated life: ~20,000 hours
- Notes: Includes a built-in humidity sensor, which lets you apply a correction.
  After applying the published correction curve, R-squared rose to 0.91.
  Fan noise is audible at close range.
- Verdict: best value.

SENSOR 3: KESTREL AIR PRO ($62)
- Interface: I2C, UART, USB
- R-squared: 0.93 overall; 0.88 when humidity > 85%
- MAE: 2.4 ug/m3
- Power: 120 mA
- Rated life: ~30,000 hours
- Notes: Dual laser channels with automatic drift check. Ships with a factory
  calibration certificate. Needs a level shifter on some 3.3 V boards.
  Backorders of 3-5 weeks reported in August.
- Verdict: closest to reference, but cost and lead time matter.

COMMON PROBLEMS
- All three drift upward after ~6 months in dusty places; clean the inlet.
- Do not mount in direct sun; heat distorts readings.
- Short sampling windows (<10 s) are noisy; average at least 1 minute.
- Do not compare readings across sensors without co-locating them first.

CITATION NOTE
If you cite these results, cite the dataset (DOI 10.0000/example.openair.2026.07)
rather than the summary page.

BOTTOM LINE
Budget under $20: Nimbus PM-3, with caveats.
Need credible data on a student budget: AeroSense S5 with humidity correction.
Need near-reference quality and can wait: Kestrel Air Pro.

Related guides: Calibrating PM sensors at home; Logging data with a Raspberry Pi; Interpreting AQI.

Get the AeroSense S5 ($29), which fits your $35 budget. It scored R-squared 0.86 against the reference monitor (MAE 3.9 ug/m3). Its built-in humidity sensor lets you apply the published correction, which raised R-squared to 0.91. The Nimbus PM-3 ($14) is much less accurate, at 0.71 and only 0.52 in humid conditions. The Kestrel Air Pro ($62) is the most accurate but over budget and backordered 3-5 weeks. Since you can't afford a second sensor for indoor/outdoor comparison, take your readings one location at a time. Average at least a minute per reading, keep the sensor out of direct sun, and cite the dataset (DOI 10.0000/example.openair.2026.07) rather than the guide page.

why does this keep old stuff between calls?? 

def add_item(item, items=[]):
    items.append(item)
    return items

add_item('a') -> ['a'], then add_item('b') -> ['a','b']

Python evaluates default argument values once, when the function is defined, not on each call. So `items=[]` creates one list that every call without an `items` argument shares and mutates.

The usual fix:

def add_item(item, items=None):
    if items is None:
        items = []
    items.append(item)
    return items
does that happen with dicts and sets too

Yes, any mutable default (list, dict, set, or your own objects) is shared the same way. Immutable defaults like ints, strings, tuples and None are safe because they can't be changed in place. In a dataclass, use `field(default_factory=list)` for the same reason.

Four good candidates:

2. Human Exposure to Microplastics via Drinking Water: Evidence and Gaps. https://www.example.org/reviews/exposure-drinking-water
